name.text: What the automorphism group Aut(f) is

questiontext.text: In the Group Theory Testing explorer, what is the automorphism group Aut(f) of a Boolean formula f?

answer.text: The set of all permutations of the variables that leave the formula's truth table unchanged

feedback.text: Correct — Aut(f) collects every relabelling of the variables that preserves f on every input row.

answer.text: The set of all input rows for which the formula evaluates to true

feedback.text: That is the on-set of the formula, not a group of permutations.

answer.text: The list of all sub-formulas appearing inside f

feedback.text: Aut(f) is about symmetries of the variables, not a syntax tree of sub-formulas.

answer.text: The number of AND, OR and NOT operators in f

feedback.text: That is a syntactic size measure; Aut(f) is a group of variable permutations.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer computes Aut(f) as every permutation of the variables that maps the truth table onto itself. It is a subgroup of the symmetric group Sₙ on the n variables, and its size is shown as |Aut(f)|.

questiontext.text: A set with an operation is a group when it satisfies which four axioms?

answer.text: Closure, associativity, identity, and inverse

feedback.text: Correct — these are exactly the four group axioms.

answer.text: Closure, commutativity, identity, and distributivity

feedback.text: Commutativity and distributivity are not required for a group; associativity and inverses are.

answer.text: Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and closure

feedback.text: Those are properties of an equivalence relation, not the group axioms.

answer.text: Identity, inverse, distributivity, and ordering

feedback.text: Distributivity and ordering are not group axioms; closure and associativity are missing.

generalfeedback.text: A group must be closed under its operation, the operation must be associative, there must be an identity element, and every element must have an inverse. Aut(f) satisfies all four under composition of permutations.

questiontext.text: The explorer always lists one element as id. What is this identity element of Aut(f)?

answer.text: The permutation that leaves every variable in place (relabels nothing)

feedback.text: Correct — id is the do-nothing permutation, the identity of the group.

answer.text: The permutation that swaps the first two variables

feedback.text: That is a transposition, not the identity.

answer.text: The input row where every variable is false

feedback.text: An input row is not a group element; the identity is the do-nothing permutation.

answer.text: The formula that is always true

feedback.text: The identity is a permutation, not a formula.

generalfeedback.text: Every group has an identity element e with e·g = g·e = g for all g. In Aut(f) that element is id, the permutation that keeps every variable in its original position. The explorer always shows it, even when the group is otherwise trivial.

name.text: What the order of a group means

questiontext.text: The panel shows Order |Aut(f)| = n. What does the order of a group mean?

answer.text: The number of elements in the group

feedback.text: Correct — the order of a finite group is its number of elements.

answer.text: The number of variables in the formula

feedback.text: That is n, the degree of Sₙ; the group's order counts permutations that preserve f, which may be smaller.

answer.text: The length of the longest cycle in any element

feedback.text: That describes an element's cycle structure, not the group's order.

answer.text: The number of orbits in the truth table

feedback.text: Orbit count is a separate quantity; the order is the number of group elements.

generalfeedback.text: The order of a finite group is simply how many elements it contains. For Aut(f) it is written |Aut(f)| and equals the number of variable permutations that leave the truth table unchanged (id always counts as one).

questiontext.text: The inverse axiom says every group element g has an inverse g⁻¹. What must g⁻¹ satisfy?

answer.text: Composing g with g⁻¹ gives the identity element

feedback.text: Correct — g · g⁻¹ = g⁻¹ · g = id.

answer.text: g⁻¹ is the largest element of the group

feedback.text: Groups need not be ordered; the inverse is defined by composing to the identity.

answer.text: g⁻¹ maps every variable to false

feedback.text: The inverse is a permutation defined by g · g⁻¹ = id, not a fixed truth assignment.

answer.text: g⁻¹ is any other element different from g

feedback.text: Only the specific element that composes with g to id is its inverse.

generalfeedback.text: For each element g the inverse g⁻¹ is the element that undoes it: g · g⁻¹ = g⁻¹ · g = id. In Aut(f) the inverse of a variable permutation is the permutation that relabels the variables back to their original positions.

questiontext.text: What is the operation that combines two elements of Aut(f)?

answer.text: Composition of the two variable permutations (apply one, then the other)

feedback.text: Correct — the group operation is function composition of permutations.

answer.text: Logical AND of the two permutations

feedback.text: AND is a Boolean connective on values, not the operation on permutations.

answer.text: Adding the number of variables each permutation moves

feedback.text: The operation composes permutations; it does not add counts.

answer.text: Taking the union of their truth tables

feedback.text: Permutations are composed as functions; truth tables are not unioned.

generalfeedback.text: Aut(f) is a group under composition: combining two symmetries means applying one permutation and then the other, which yields another permutation that also preserves the truth table.

questiontext.text: In the Orbit Explorer, what is an orbit?

answer.text: A set of truth-table rows that the group's permutations map onto one another

feedback.text: Correct — an orbit groups all rows reachable from one another by applying Aut(f).

answer.text: A single row of the truth table chosen at random

feedback.text: An orbit is a whole set of mutually reachable rows, not one random row.

answer.text: The list of variables that appear in the formula

feedback.text: Those are the variables; an orbit is a set of truth-table rows under the group action.

answer.text: The set of operators used to build the formula

feedback.text: Operators are syntax; an orbit is a symmetry class of input rows.

generalfeedback.text: Acting with Aut(f) on the truth table partitions its rows into orbits: two rows are in the same orbit when some symmetry of f maps one to the other. Rows in one orbit always share the same f value and the same colour in the table.

questiontext.text: For the preset formula A AND B, the explorer reports how many elements in Aut(f)?

feedback.text: Correct — Aut(A AND B) = {id, (AB)}, order 2, because AND is symmetric in A and B.
Order 1 would mean no symmetry, but swapping A and B leaves A AND B unchanged, so there are two elements.
4 is the number of truth-table rows (2²), not the group order.
6 is |Aut| for the 3-variable majority formula, not for A AND B.

generalfeedback.text: Because A AND B is symmetric, swapping A and B preserves the truth table. Aut(f) therefore contains id and the transposition (AB), giving order 2 — which is the full symmetric group S₂ on two variables.

questiontext.text: For the preset A AND NOT B, the panel says "No variable symmetry". What is |Aut(f)|?

answer.text: 1 — only the identity id is in the group

feedback.text: Correct — no non-trivial permutation preserves A AND NOT B, so Aut(f) = {id}, order 1.

answer.text: 2 — id and the swap (AB)

feedback.text: Swapping A and B changes the truth table here, so (AB) is not an automorphism.

answer.text: 0 — the group is empty

feedback.text: A group is never empty; it always contains at least the identity.

answer.text: 4 — every row is its own orbit

feedback.text: 4 is the number of orbits (all singletons), not the group order.

generalfeedback.text: A AND NOT B treats A and B differently, so swapping them changes the truth table and is not a symmetry. Only id remains, so |Aut(f)| = 1 — the trivial group — and every input row forms its own orbit.

name.text: Reading a value off the orbit table

questiontext.text: In the orbit table for A AND B, what is f(x) in the row where A=T and B=T?

answer.text: T

feedback.text: Correct — A AND B is true only when both are true, so the T,T row gives f = T.

answer.text: F

feedback.text: Both variables are true, so A AND B is true, not false.

answer.text: It depends on the orbit colour

feedback.text: The colour shows the orbit, but f(x) is a fixed value read from the table; here it is T.

answer.text: Undefined

feedback.text: Every row has a defined f value; for T,T it is T.

generalfeedback.text: The f(x) column shows the formula's value for each input row. For A AND B, only the row A=T, B=T evaluates to T; the other three rows are F.

questiontext.text: In the orbit table, what does the ★ Rep mark on a row mean?

answer.text: That row is the chosen representative of its orbit (the smallest row index)

feedback.text: Correct — ★ marks the representative, and the explorer picks the smallest-index row in each orbit.

answer.text: That row makes the formula true

feedback.text: ★ marks the orbit representative, unrelated to whether f is true there.

answer.text: That row can be deleted from the truth table

feedback.text: The representative is the one you keep as a test; the non-starred rows in its orbit are the ones it stands in for.

answer.text: That row belongs to no orbit

feedback.text: Every row belongs to an orbit; ★ marks the representative of one.

generalfeedback.text: Each orbit is collapsed to a single representative test. The explorer marks that representative with ★ and chooses the row with the smallest index in the orbit, so testing just the starred rows covers every symmetry class.

questiontext.text: The explorer lists a non-identity element as (AB). In cycle notation, what does (AB) mean?

answer.text: A permutation that swaps variables A and B and fixes the rest

feedback.text: Correct — the 2-cycle (AB) exchanges A and B, leaving other variables in place.

answer.text: The logical AND of A and B

feedback.text: (AB) is a permutation in cycle notation, not a Boolean AND.

answer.text: An orbit containing rows A and B

feedback.text: Cycle notation describes a permutation, not an orbit of rows.

answer.text: A formula equal to A followed by B

feedback.text: It is a permutation that swaps two variables, not a formula.

generalfeedback.text: Cycle notation (AB) denotes the permutation that sends A to B and B to A while leaving every other variable unmoved. The explorer prints each non-identity symmetry this way; a lone id means no non-trivial symmetry.

questiontext.text: The automorphism group Aut(f) of an n-variable formula is a subgroup of which group?

answer.text: The symmetric group Sₙ of all permutations of the n variables

feedback.text: Correct — Aut(f) consists of those permutations in Sₙ that preserve the truth table.

answer.text: The additive group of integers

feedback.text: Aut(f) is a group of variable permutations, a subgroup of Sₙ, not of the integers.

answer.text: The group of rows of the truth table under XOR

feedback.text: Aut(f) acts on rows but its elements are permutations of variables, sitting inside Sₙ.

answer.text: The multiplicative group of GF(p)

feedback.text: GF(p) appears in the covering-array tab; Aut(f) is a subgroup of Sₙ.

generalfeedback.text: Every element of Aut(f) permutes the n variables, so Aut(f) is a subset of Sₙ, the group of all n! permutations. Because it is closed, contains id, and has inverses, it is a subgroup of Sₙ.

name.text: Covering array alphabet must be prime

questiontext.text: In the Covering Array tab, the alphabet size p for the GF(p) construction must be a prime number.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the construction uses the finite field GF(p), which requires p to be prime (the tab offers 2, 3, 5).

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The GF(p) construction relies on a finite field of order p, so p must be prime.

generalfeedback.text: The orthogonal-array construction in the explorer works over the finite field GF(p), which exists only when p is prime (or a prime power). The tab restricts p to the primes 2, 3, and 5.

questiontext.text: The majority formula (A∧B)∨(B∧C)∨(A∧C) has three variables. How many rows does its truth table have?

feedback.text: Correct — with n = 3 variables there are 2³ = 8 input rows.
3 is the number of variables, not the number of rows.
6 is |Aut(f)| for this formula, not the number of rows.
9 is a covering-array row count for GF(3); the truth table has 2³ = 8 rows.

generalfeedback.text: A Boolean formula with n variables has a truth table of 2ⁿ rows. For the 3-variable majority formula that is 2³ = 8 rows, which the explorer then partitions into orbits.

questiontext.text: Why does the closure axiom hold for Aut(f): composing two symmetries of f gives an element of Aut(f)?

answer.text: If each permutation leaves the truth table unchanged, applying them in turn also leaves it unchanged, so the composition preserves f too

feedback.text: Correct — preservation is preserved under composition, so the result is again a symmetry of f.

answer.text: Because any two permutations of the same variables are always equal

feedback.text: Distinct permutations are generally different; closure comes from both preserving the truth table.

answer.text: Because composition always yields the identity permutation

feedback.text: Composition usually yields a non-identity permutation; it stays inside Aut(f) because f is preserved.

answer.text: Because the truth table has an even number of rows

feedback.text: The row count is irrelevant; closure follows from both permutations preserving f.

generalfeedback.text: If g and h each map the truth table onto itself, then applying g and then h still maps it onto itself. So g·h also preserves f and is again in Aut(f). This is exactly the closure axiom, and it is why Aut(f) is a group under composition.

questiontext.text: For the majority formula (A∧B)∨(B∧C)∨(A∧C), what is |Aut(f)|?

answer.text: 6 — every permutation of A, B, C preserves the formula, so Aut(f) = S₃

feedback.text: Correct — majority is fully symmetric, so all 3! = 6 permutations are automorphisms.

answer.text: 3 — only the three cyclic rotations

feedback.text: The transpositions preserve majority too, so the group is the full S₃ of order 6, not just the 3 rotations.

answer.text: 2 — only id and one swap

feedback.text: All six permutations preserve majority, so the order is 6, not 2.

answer.text: 8 — one per truth-table row

feedback.text: 8 is the number of rows; |Aut(f)| counts symmetries and equals 6.

generalfeedback.text: Majority-of-three is symmetric in all three variables: any relabelling of A, B, C leaves the truth table unchanged. Hence Aut(f) is the entire symmetric group S₃, of order 3! = 6.

name.text: Why A AND NOT B has no symmetry

questiontext.text: Why is Aut(A AND NOT B) trivial (order 1)?

answer.text: Swapping A and B changes the truth table, so the swap is not an automorphism and only id remains

feedback.text: Correct — A and B play different roles, so exchanging them alters f and cannot be a symmetry.

answer.text: The formula is always false, so it has no symmetry

feedback.text: A AND NOT B is true when A=T, B=F; it is not constant. The lack of symmetry is because A and B differ in role.

answer.text: NOT is not allowed inside an automorphism

feedback.text: NOT is fine in the formula; the point is that swapping the variables changes the truth table.

answer.text: Because it has only two variables

feedback.text: A AND B also has two variables yet has a non-trivial symmetry; the asymmetry is due to the differing roles of A and B.

generalfeedback.text: In A AND NOT B the two variables are not interchangeable: A must be true and B false to satisfy f. Swapping them yields B AND NOT A, a different truth table, so (AB) is not a symmetry. Only id survives, giving the trivial group.

name.text: Number of orbits for A AND B

questiontext.text: For A AND B, into how many orbits does Aut(f) partition the 4 truth-table rows?

feedback.text: Correct — the orbits are {F,F}, {F,T ; T,F}, and {T,T}: three classes.
The swap symmetry merges the rows F,T and T,F, so there are 3 orbits, not 4.
Only the two mixed rows merge; the F,F and T,T rows stay separate, giving 3 orbits.
Rows with different f values cannot share an orbit, so there is more than one.

generalfeedback.text: The symmetry (AB) fixes F,F and T,T but swaps the two mixed rows F,T and T,F into one orbit. That gives three orbits — one fewer than the four rows — so one test is saved.

questiontext.text: What is the testing role of an orbit's representative in the explorer?

answer.text: It is the single test kept for the whole orbit, since all rows in the orbit are symmetry-equivalent

feedback.text: Correct — one representative per orbit suffices because its orbit-mates carry the same test obligation.

answer.text: It is the row most likely to reveal a fault

feedback.text: The representative is chosen by smallest index, not by fault likelihood; it simply stands in for its orbit.

answer.text: It is the row that must never be tested

feedback.text: The opposite — the representative is exactly the row you do test for that orbit.

answer.text: It is the identity element of the group

feedback.text: The identity is a permutation; a representative is a truth-table row.

generalfeedback.text: Rows in the same orbit are related by a symmetry of f, so they share the same test obligation. Keeping one representative per orbit collapses the equivalent rows into a single test, which is how the group reduces the required test count.

questiontext.text: For A AND B, the orbit {A=F,B=T ; A=T,B=F} yields which metamorphic relation shown by the explorer?

answer.text: f(A=F, B=T) = f(A=T, B=F)

feedback.text: Correct — rows in one orbit must give equal outputs, which is the metamorphic relation.

answer.text: f(A=F, B=T) = NOT f(A=T, B=F)

feedback.text: Orbit-mates give equal outputs, not negated ones.

answer.text: f(A=T, B=T) = f(A=F, B=F)

feedback.text: Those two rows are in different orbits (T,T and F,F) and are not related this way.

answer.text: f(A=F, B=T) = A OR B

feedback.text: A metamorphic relation equates two runs of the same function, not the function with a different formula.

generalfeedback.text: Because a symmetry of f maps one orbit-mate to the other, the formula must give the same value on both. The explorer turns each orbit into a metamorphic relation of the form f(row₁) = f(row₂), here f(A=F,B=T) = f(A=T,B=F).

questiontext.text: In Aut(f), what is the inverse of the transposition (AB)?

answer.text: (AB) itself — a swap is its own inverse

feedback.text: Correct — applying (AB) twice restores the original, so (AB)⁻¹ = (AB).

answer.text: id — the identity is its own inverse and everyone else's

feedback.text: id is only its own inverse; (AB) undoes itself, not id.

answer.text: A 3-cycle (ABC)

feedback.text: A 3-cycle is not the inverse of a 2-cycle; a swap is its own inverse.

answer.text: (AB) has no inverse

feedback.text: Every group element has an inverse; for a transposition it is the transposition itself.

generalfeedback.text: Swapping A and B and then swapping again returns every variable to its place: (AB)·(AB) = id. So a transposition is its own inverse and has order 2.

questiontext.text: In the Covering Array tab with alphabet p = 3 and strength t = 2, how many test rows does the GF(p) construction produce?

feedback.text: Correct — a strength-2 array over GF(3) has p² = 9 rows.
3 rows is the strength-1 (t=1) case; strength 2 needs p² = 9.
6 is not p²; the strength-2 construction over GF(3) gives 9 rows.
27 = 3³ is an exhaustive count for three parameters; the OA needs only p² = 9 rows.

generalfeedback.text: For strength t = 2 the GF(p) orthogonal-array construction uses p² rows. With p = 3 that is 9 test rows, which still guarantees every pair of values across the parameters is covered.

name.text: Orbit count for the majority formula

questiontext.text: For (A∧B)∨(B∧C)∨(A∧C), how many orbits does S₃ create among the 8 truth-table rows?

feedback.text: Correct — the orbits group rows by how many variables are true: 0, 1, 2, or 3.
Full symmetry merges rows, so there are fewer than 8 orbits.
6 is |Aut(f)|; the number of orbits is 4.
There are four orbits (weights 0,1,2,3), not two.

generalfeedback.text: Because every permutation of the variables is a symmetry, two rows are in the same orbit exactly when they have the same number of true variables. The possible counts 0, 1, 2, 3 give four orbits (sizes 1, 3, 3, 1).

name.text: Why symmetry reduces the test count

questiontext.text: Why can rows sharing the same orbit colour be collapsed into one test?

answer.text: They are related by a symmetry of f, so they share the same test obligation — testing one covers the rest

feedback.text: Correct — symmetry-equivalent inputs impose the same obligation, so one representative suffices.

answer.text: They always evaluate to false, so they need not be tested

feedback.text: Orbit-mates can be true or false; they are collapsed because they are symmetry-equivalent, not because they are false.

answer.text: They are duplicate rows literally repeated in the table

feedback.text: The rows are distinct inputs; they are equivalent only under the group's symmetry.

answer.text: They are outside the formula's domain

feedback.text: All rows are valid inputs; they are merged because a symmetry maps one to another.

generalfeedback.text: A symmetry of f maps one orbit-mate onto another while preserving the output, so the rows carry identical test obligations. Exercising a single representative therefore discharges the obligation for the whole orbit, which is the saving the explorer reports.

name.text: Meaning of a derived CACC pair

questiontext.text: In the CACC Bridge tab, what does a pair labelled ✓ Derived (free) mean?

answer.text: It is the orbit-image of a seed pair, so the required test is already covered and no extra test is needed

feedback.text: Correct — a derived pair is a symmetry image of a seed pair, so it costs no additional test.

answer.text: It is a pair that can be ignored because it never changes the outcome

feedback.text: Determination pairs do change the outcome; a derived pair is still exercised, just for free via symmetry.

answer.text: It is a pair with no relationship to any other pair

feedback.text: A derived pair is precisely related — it is the orbit image of a seed pair.

answer.text: It is a syntactically invalid pair

feedback.text: Derived pairs are valid determination pairs; they are simply covered by a seed pair's symmetry.

generalfeedback.text: Seed pairs must be tested independently. A derived pair is a symmetry (orbit) image of a seed pair, so the same relabelling that proves the seed also discharges the derived one — the required test is already covered, hence "free".

name.text: Why a set can fail to be a group

questiontext.text: The set of permutations {(AB)} (a single swap, without id) is not a group. Which axiom fails first?

answer.text: Identity — the set does not contain the identity element id

feedback.text: Correct — a group must contain the identity, and {(AB)} does not.

answer.text: Associativity — composition of permutations is not associative

feedback.text: Composition of permutations is always associative; the missing element is the identity.

answer.text: Commutativity — the swap does not commute with itself

feedback.text: Commutativity is not a group axiom, and any element commutes with itself anyway.

answer.text: Nothing fails; it is already a group

feedback.text: It cannot be a group: it lacks the identity (and is not closed, since (AB)·(AB) = id is absent).

generalfeedback.text: Every group must contain an identity element. The set {(AB)} has no id, so it fails the identity axiom; it is also not closed, since (AB)·(AB) = id is not in the set. Adding id gives {id, (AB)}, which is a valid group of order 2.

questiontext.text: For a strength t = 2 covering array over GF(p), the explorer caps the number of parameters k. What is the cap?

answer.text: k ≤ p + 1

feedback.text: Correct — the standard GF(p) construction supports up to p + 1 parameters at strength 2.

answer.text: k ≤ p − 1

feedback.text: The construction allows one more than that: up to p + 1 parameters.

answer.text: k ≤ p²

feedback.text: p² is the row count, not the parameter cap; the cap is p + 1.

answer.text: There is no cap

feedback.text: The GF(p) construction limits k to p + 1 at strength 2, and the explorer warns when k exceeds it.

generalfeedback.text: The GF(p)-based orthogonal-array construction can cover up to p + 1 mutually orthogonal parameters at strength 2. Beyond that the field runs out of independent slopes, so the explorer caps k at p + 1 and shows a warning.

name.text: Which rows share the orbit of TFF in majority

questiontext.text: In the majority formula, the row A=T, B=F, C=F is in the same orbit as which rows?

answer.text: The other two rows with exactly one true variable: F,F,T and F,T,F

feedback.text: Correct — S₃ permutes the single true variable to any position, so all weight-1 rows share one orbit.

answer.text: The row T,T,T only

feedback.text: T,T,T has three trues (weight 3); it is in a different orbit from a weight-1 row.

answer.text: The rows with two true variables

feedback.text: Weight-2 rows form a separate orbit; T,F,F has weight 1.

answer.text: No other rows — it is alone in its orbit

feedback.text: Under full symmetry all three weight-1 rows merge, so it is not alone.

generalfeedback.text: Under S₃, rows are equivalent exactly when they have the same number of true variables. The row T,F,F has one true variable, so its orbit is all weight-1 rows: T,F,F, F,T,F, and F,F,T.

name.text: Orbit equality is a metamorphic relation

questiontext.text: The explorer treats the equality of f across the rows of one orbit, f(x) = f(σx) for a symmetry σ, as a metamorphic relation, and even offers a bridge to the Metamorphic Testing explorer.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — orbit-mates must give equal outputs, which is exactly a metamorphic relation the tool exports.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The tool does derive metamorphic relations from orbits and links to the Metamorphic Testing explorer to verify them.

generalfeedback.text: Because a symmetry σ of f maps a row x to σx without changing the output, f(x) = f(σx) must hold. This is a metamorphic relation, and the explorer lists these relations from orbits and provides a bridge button to the Metamorphic Testing explorer.

questiontext.text: In S₃ = Aut(majority), composing the two transpositions (AB) and (AC) yields what kind of element?

answer.text: A 3-cycle (a rotation of all three variables)

feedback.text: Correct — the product of two distinct transpositions in S₃ is a 3-cycle.

answer.text: The identity id

feedback.text: Composing a transposition with itself gives id, but (AB) and (AC) are different, so the product is a 3-cycle.

answer.text: Another transposition

feedback.text: Two distinct transpositions compose to a 3-cycle, not a transposition.

answer.text: An element outside the group

feedback.text: By closure the product stays inside S₃; it is the 3-cycle.

generalfeedback.text: In S₃ the product of two distinct transpositions is always a 3-cycle. This is why {id, (AB), (AC)} is not closed — composing its two swaps produces a rotation that the set does not contain.

questiontext.text: What is the order of the element (ABC) in Aut(majority) — the smallest k with (ABC)ᵏ = id?

feedback.text: Correct — a 3-cycle returns to the identity only after being applied three times.
Applying a 3-cycle twice gives another 3-cycle (its inverse), not id; the order is 3.
6 is the group's order; the element (ABC) has order 3.
Only id has order 1; (ABC) is non-trivial, with order 3.

generalfeedback.text: The order of an element is the smallest positive k with gᵏ = id. Rotating three variables once gives (ABC), twice gives (ACB), and three times returns everything to place, so the order of a 3-cycle is 3.

questiontext.text: Which subset of Aut(majority) = S₃ is itself a subgroup?

answer.text: {id, (ABC), (ACB)} — the two rotations together with id

feedback.text: Correct — this is the cyclic group of order 3 (the alternating group A₃), closed under composition.

answer.text: {id, (AB), (AC)}

feedback.text: Not closed — composing (AB) and (AC) gives a 3-cycle that is not in the set.
This lacks id and is not closed (a product of two transpositions is a 3-cycle), so it is not a subgroup.

answer.text: {id, (AB), (AC), (BC)}

feedback.text: Not closed — (AB)·(AC) is a 3-cycle outside the set — and its size 4 does not divide 6.

generalfeedback.text: {id, (ABC), (ACB)} is closed (each product of rotations is again a rotation or id), contains id, and has inverses ((ABC)⁻¹ = (ACB)). It is the order-3 cyclic subgroup A₃. The other sets are not closed or lack id.

questiontext.text: Aut(f) is a subgroup of Sₙ, so by Lagrange's theorem |Aut(f)| divides n!. For a 3-variable formula, which value can not be |Aut(f)|?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 does not divide 3! = 6, so it cannot be the order of a subgroup of S₃.
1 divides 6 (the trivial group), so it is a possible order.
2 divides 6, so an order-2 subgroup is possible.
6 divides 6 — this is the full group S₃, e.g. for majority.

generalfeedback.text: By Lagrange's theorem the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group. For S₃, |S₃| = 6, so subgroup orders must divide 6: the possibilities are 1, 2, 3, 6. Since 4 does not divide 6, |Aut(f)| can never be 4 for a 3-variable formula.

name.text: Orbits of a fully symmetric function

questiontext.text: If an n-variable formula is fully symmetric (Aut(f) = Sₙ), how many orbits does it have on the truth table, and why?

answer.text: n + 1 orbits — one per possible number of true variables (Hamming weight 0 through n)

feedback.text: Correct — Sₙ merges all rows of equal weight, giving one orbit for each weight 0..n.

answer.text: 2ⁿ orbits — every row stays separate

feedback.text: Full symmetry merges rows of equal weight, so there are far fewer than 2ⁿ orbits.

answer.text: n orbits — one per variable

feedback.text: The orbits are indexed by weight 0..n, which is n + 1 classes, not n.

answer.text: 2 orbits — true rows and false rows

feedback.text: Rows split by weight, not merely by output; there are n + 1 orbits.

generalfeedback.text: Under the full symmetric group, two truth-table rows are equivalent exactly when they have the same number of true variables. The weight ranges from 0 to n, giving n + 1 orbits. For n = 3 (majority) that is 4 orbits, matching the explorer.

name.text: Tests saved by the majority group

questiontext.text: For majority-of-three (8 rows, 4 orbits), how many tests does the symmetry save, as reported by the explorer?

answer.text: 4 — keep 4 representatives instead of all 8 rows

feedback.text: Correct — 8 rows collapse to 4 orbit representatives, saving 8 − 4 = 4 tests.
The saving is rows minus orbits = 8 − 4 = 4, not 2.
6 is |Aut(f)|; the tests saved equal 8 − 4 = 4.
Symmetry does reduce the count here: from 8 rows to 4 orbits, saving 4.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer reports "Saves N tests" where N = total rows − orbit representatives. For majority that is 8 − 4 = 4: only the four weight-classes need a representative test.

name.text: CACC seed and derived pairs for A AND B

questiontext.text: For A AND B, the CACC Bridge finds 2 determination pairs in total. How many are derived for free by symmetry, and how many are seeds?

answer.text: 1 seed and 1 derived — the A-pair seeds it and the B-pair is its orbit image via the A↔B swap

feedback.text: Correct — the swap symmetry maps the A determination pair onto the B one, so only one seed is needed.

answer.text: 2 seeds and 0 derived

feedback.text: The A↔B symmetry derives the second pair for free, so there is 1 seed and 1 derived.

answer.text: 0 seeds and 2 derived

feedback.text: At least one pair must be an independent seed; here it is 1 seed and 1 derived.

answer.text: 1 seed and 0 derived

feedback.text: There are 2 pairs total; the second is derived, giving 1 seed and 1 derived.

generalfeedback.text: A AND B has one determination pair for A and one for B. Processing A first makes its pair a seed; the swap (AB) maps that pair onto B's pair, marking it derived. So 1 seed plus 1 derived — the symmetry halves the independent CACC obligation.

questiontext.text: In Aut(f), the order of any element must divide the order of the group |Aut(f)|.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — this is a corollary of Lagrange's theorem: an element generates a cyclic subgroup whose order divides |Aut(f)|.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The order of an element equals the size of the cyclic subgroup it generates, which by Lagrange divides the group order.

generalfeedback.text: An element g generates the cyclic subgroup {id, g, g², …} whose size is the order of g. By Lagrange's theorem this size divides |Aut(f)|. In S₃ (order 6), element orders are 1, 2, and 3 — all divisors of 6.

questiontext.text: In the Covering Array tab with p = 3, k = 4, t = 2, the explorer names the array OA(9; 2, 4, 3). What does it guarantee?

answer.text: Its 9 rows cover every 2-way combination of the 4 parameters over the 3 values

feedback.text: Correct — a strength-2 OA with these parameters covers all pairwise value combinations in 9 rows.

answer.text: Its 9 rows cover every 3-way combination of the parameters

feedback.text: Strength t = 2 guarantees 2-way (pairwise) coverage, not 3-way.

answer.text: It lists all 3⁴ = 81 combinations exhaustively

feedback.text: The point of the OA is to avoid exhaustive testing: 9 rows suffice for pairwise coverage instead of 81.

answer.text: It covers only the single most important parameter

feedback.text: It covers all pairs across all four parameters, not just one.

generalfeedback.text: In OA(N; t, k, p), N is the row count, t the strength, k the number of parameters, and p the alphabet size. OA(9; 2, 4, 3) uses 9 rows to guarantee that every pair of values among the 4 parameters (each over 3 values) appears together in some row.

questiontext.text: For p = 3, k = 4, t = 2, how many distinct 2-way (pairwise) value combinations must the covering array cover in total?

feedback.text: Correct — there are C(4,2) = 6 column pairs, each with p² = 9 value combinations: 6 × 9 = 54.
9 is the number of value combinations for one column pair (p²), not across all 6 pairs.
That would use 4 column pairs; there are C(4,2) = 6 pairs, giving 6 × 9 = 54.
81 = 3⁴ is the exhaustive number of full rows, not the count of 2-way combinations.

generalfeedback.text: The number of pairwise combinations is (number of column pairs) × pᵗ = C(k,2) × p². With k = 4 and p = 3 that is 6 × 9 = 54 distinct 2-way value combinations, all covered by the 9-row OA.

questiontext.text: Why is {id, (AB), (AC)} not a subgroup of S₃?

answer.text: It is not closed: composing (AB) and (AC) gives a 3-cycle that is not in the set

feedback.text: Correct — closure fails, so the subset is not a subgroup.

answer.text: It lacks the identity element

feedback.text: It does contain id; the failure is closure, not the identity.

answer.text: Its elements have no inverses

feedback.text: Each transposition is its own inverse; the problem is that closure fails.

answer.text: Composition of permutations is not associative

feedback.text: Composition is always associative; the subset simply is not closed.

generalfeedback.text: A subgroup must be closed. But (AB)·(AC) is a 3-cycle, which is not among {id, (AB), (AC)}. Since applying the operation leaves the set, closure fails and it cannot be a subgroup — its size 3 would be allowed by Lagrange, but closure still fails.

questiontext.text: Comparing (A∧B)∨(B∧C)∨(A∧C) with A AND NOT B, why does the first have |Aut(f)| = 6 while the second has |Aut(f)| = 1?

answer.text: Majority treats all variables interchangeably (every permutation preserves it), while A AND NOT B assigns distinct roles, so no non-trivial permutation preserves it

feedback.text: Correct — the more interchangeable the variables, the larger Aut(f); asymmetric roles collapse it to id.

answer.text: Majority has more operators, and operator count sets the group size

feedback.text: Group size reflects variable symmetry, not the number of operators.

answer.text: A AND NOT B has fewer variables, and fewer variables always means order 1

feedback.text: A AND B also has two variables yet has order 2; the difference is symmetry of roles, not variable count.

answer.text: Majority is always true, so all permutations trivially preserve it

feedback.text: Majority is not constant; permutations preserve it because the variables are interchangeable.

generalfeedback.text: |Aut(f)| measures how interchangeable the variables are. In majority every variable plays the same role, so all 3! = 6 permutations preserve the truth table. In A AND NOT B the variables have opposite roles, so only id survives and |Aut(f)| = 1.

name.text: Metamorphic relation from a majority orbit

questiontext.text: For majority, the orbit {F,F,T ; F,T,F ; T,F,F} gives the metamorphic relation maj(F,F,T) = maj(F,T,F) = maj(T,F,F). What common value do these outputs share?

answer.text: F — each input has only one true variable, so the majority is false

feedback.text: Correct — with just one variable true, fewer than half are true, so majority is F for all three.

answer.text: T — a majority orbit is always true

feedback.text: Weight-1 rows have only one true variable, so the majority is F, not T.

answer.text: The three outputs differ from one another

feedback.text: Orbit-mates must share a value; here they are all F, which is why they form a metamorphic relation.

answer.text: Undefined, because the inputs differ

feedback.text: The outputs are all defined and equal to F; the differing inputs are related by symmetry.

generalfeedback.text: Majority-of-three is true only when at least two variables are true. Each row in this orbit has exactly one true variable, so all three evaluate to F. Being in one orbit, they must share a value — which the metamorphic relation records as maj(F,F,T) = maj(F,T,F) = maj(T,F,F) = F.

questiontext.text: For two elements g, h of Aut(f), what is the inverse of their composition (g·h)⁻¹?

answer.text: h⁻¹·g⁻¹ — the inverses in reverse order

feedback.text: Correct — undoing g then h means undoing h first, then g: (g·h)⁻¹ = h⁻¹·g⁻¹.

answer.text: g⁻¹·h⁻¹ — the inverses in the same order

feedback.text: The order must reverse; (g·h)⁻¹ = h⁻¹·g⁻¹, not g⁻¹·h⁻¹ (unless they commute).

answer.text: g·h again

feedback.text: That would only equal the inverse if g·h had order 2; in general the inverse is h⁻¹·g⁻¹.

answer.text: id, because compositions are always self-inverse

feedback.text: Compositions are not generally self-inverse; the inverse is h⁻¹·g⁻¹.

generalfeedback.text: The "socks and shoes" rule: to undo applying g then h, you must undo h first, then g. So (g·h)⁻¹ = h⁻¹·g⁻¹. For transpositions, which are self-inverse, this becomes (g·h)⁻¹ = h·g.

name.text: How the symmetry group cuts test obligations

questiontext.text: Across the explorer's tabs, how does the symmetry group Aut(f) reduce testing effort overall?

answer.text: It collapses symmetry-equivalent truth-table rows into one orbit representative and derives CACC pairs as orbit images, and these orbit equalities become metamorphic relations to verify

feedback.text: Correct — orbits reduce rows, symmetry derives CACC pairs for free, and orbit equalities export as metamorphic relations.

answer.text: It proves the program correct without any testing

feedback.text: Group symmetry reduces and relates tests; it never proves correctness on its own.

answer.text: It removes the need for a test oracle entirely

feedback.text: The orbit equalities act as metamorphic relations — partial oracles — but do not eliminate oracles altogether.

answer.text: It increases the number of required tests to be safe

feedback.text: The whole point is a reduction: fewer representatives, derived CACC pairs, and reusable metamorphic relations.

generalfeedback.text: Aut(f) ties the three tabs together: in the Orbit Explorer it merges equivalent rows into representatives (fewer tests); in the CACC Bridge it derives determination pairs as orbit images of seeds (free coverage); and the resulting orbit equalities f(x) = f(σx) become metamorphic relations that the Metamorphic Testing explorer can verify.
